description: Test your knowledge of PA BR1 | Breast anatomy, inflammation, and benign pathology.

cards.text: What are the three key histological components of the TDLU, and which cell type confirms a benign lesion?
cards.answer: Luminal epithelial cells (produce milk, ER+/PR+), myoepithelial cells (contractile, ER-negative, sit on basement membrane), and basement membrane. Presence of the myoepithelial layer is pathognomonic for benign lesions; carcinoma destroys this layer.

tip.tip: Remember: 'MY-epithelial = Malignant lesions Yank it out' — loss of myoepithelial layer = invasion has begun

cards.text: Name the most common causative organism in acute lactational mastitis and describe the management principle.
cards.answer: Staphylococcus aureus (90% of cases). Manage with antibiotics; lactation may continue. If fluctuant/abscess present, incise and drain.

tip.tip: 90% Staph = 'STAph Starts in 90% of lactational infections' — don't stop lactation unless severe

cards.text: What is the defining histological feature that distinguishes periductal mastitis, and what clinical sign is a trap?
cards.answer: Periductal infiltrate dominated by plasma cells (hence the name). Clinical trap: nipple retraction + subareolar mass = must exclude carcinoma with triple assessment (imaging, clinical, biopsy).

tip.tip: Plasma cells = Periductal mastitis; Retraction + mass = Carcinoma until proven otherwise

cards.text: Describe the pathogenesis of periductal mastitis starting from the epithelial change.
cards.answer: Squamous metaplasia of duct epithelium → duct obstruction by squamous debris → duct ectasia and rupture → lipid leakage into periductal stroma → chemical irritation and plasma cell-rich inflammation.

tip.tip: Sequential steps: Squamous change → Duct obstruction → Ectasia → Rupture → Periductal inflammation

cards.text: What is fat necrosis and why is it a clinical and radiological trap?
cards.answer: Reactive condition from trauma (surgical, radiation, vasculitis). Closely mimics carcinoma clinically and on imaging. History of injury present in only 50% of cases, making diagnosis easily missed.

tip.tip: FAT necrosis = Fake 'carcinoma' Almost always — history of trauma often forgotten

cards.text: Contrast intralobular stroma and interlobular stroma in terms of hormone responsiveness and location.
cards.answer: Intralobular stroma: loose, hormone-responsive, surrounds the TDLU directly. Interlobular stroma: dense fibrous tissue between lobes, less hormone-responsive.

tip.tip: INtralobular = IN the TDLU, hormonally IN-tune; INterlobular = between lobes, less INterested in hormones

cards.text: Which breast hormone phases cause ductal proliferation and which cause lobular acinar budding?
cards.answer: Follicular phase (rising estrogen): ductal proliferation. Luteal phase (rising progesterone): lobular acinar budding and edema.

tip.tip: Follicular → Following ducts; Luteal → Lobular buds

cards.text: In periductal mastitis, what color is the nipple discharge and what is the underlying epithelial abnormality?
cards.answer: Nipple discharge is green or black. The underlying abnormality is squamous metaplasia of duct epithelium, which leads to duct obstruction and ectasia.

tip.tip: Green/black discharge = Dammed-up squamous debris in dilated ducts
